utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, before we continue with you as a witness, I do understand that Mr. Registrar has, to the extent finished already, that he has tried to make lists of documents provided by Mr. Krajisnik. It also shows that a great majority is already in evidence, which lessens, a bit, the urgency of the matter. And I do understand that we do not have yet translation of all of the inventory lists provided by Mr. Krajisnik, but that translation is -- I think we have one that has been translated by now and the others perhaps still to come soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll double-check. We think the position as far as what we received as far as the Court is concerned is exactly as Your Honour has said. We've done some stuff ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a look at that. Then we'll go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the things that you, Mr. Harmon, asked for is that we pay attention to the photographic material you provided at the request of the Chamber. And, Mr. Krajisnik, it was decided that you would be given an opportunity to make comments on it within the limits I set out when I delivered a decision. Mr. Harmon, I see that I have a series of photographs on my desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These photographs plus the companion sheet showing the municipality, the location, the census figures, the object of the photograph, the date of the alleged destruction, the date the photograph was taken, the -- who took the photograph, and the ERN number, that has been submitted in respect of each of the municipalities that are part of this compendium. I have taken the instructions of the Court and eliminated certain information that was contained in this according to the Court's instruction. We submit it now, Your Honour. I believe it should have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1258, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In addition to that, Your Honour, there is a CD that deals with the tour of the parts of the municipality of Prijedor that is identified at the -- should be at the end of the descriptive materials, and I would like to submit these as well to the Court. And these also should be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1259, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at one of those indexes, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These indexes -- I see this is an index of the video. But didn't you receive the -- Mr. Harmon, did Defence not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I meant that index, the index of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the video, that's a very short one. It gives the census, the object being destroyed houses, alleged date of destruction, 24th to 28th of May, 1992, the date on which the video was taken, and by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, you have been able to review this material, and as I said yesterday an opportunity -- and as a said before, as a matter of fact, an opportunity would be given to you to give comments on the matter. Please do so, and if you would -- whenever you have comment on a certain document, please give us time to find it. It's organised municipality by municipality, as I see. Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have received this material from Mr. Josse, and as you have said, I will try to express my objections in principle or, rather, to point out certain things that could be helpful to the Trial Chamber and the others. Just one general remark first. I have seen such destroyed houses after the war when I travelled throughout Republika Srpska, and although I did not travel across the Federation, I cannot say that there are not any houses destroyed in that latest war. There certainly are. And now, more specifically, this is the first photograph I received, it's 03265854. It's a rather large house, demolished, destroyed. What I wanted to emphasise and what could have confused the person who took this photo, if this photo was taken to prove that Serbs had destroyed this house - because I don't think the intent was to show Serbian destroyed houses - however I know from practice that there are Muslim symbols there, the coat of arms of Muslims, the half crescent, letters SDA, and a word "apapusa" instead of "arapusa." And there is another inscription in Roman script. What I want to say is this: What happened in the war is that whichever army passed through a settlement would leave their emblems and inscriptions. Serbs would draw crosses or SDS, Croats would write something different like HDZ. I don't think that this particular destruction was committed by Serbs because I see only one Serb house here, but from my experience I would not say that the Serb side destroyed this because they would not have written SDA, although "arapusa," as far as I know, is a predominantly Muslim settlement. I have seen in many settlements belonging to other ethnic communities where the Serb army passed through, you can see Serb inscriptions, whereas in other settlements that had been seized by the Muslim army you can see the traces of that ethnic community, of that army. On another photograph we see a date, 25th of July, 2001, and the photograph depicts a house, complete with a roof. I haven't written down the number. It's a house under a roof, an electrical transmission pillar next to it. I see there is another structure there, like an outhouse, but the house bears no trace of destruction. So maybe it was just the mine, a shell, that fell on it. What I'm trying to say is that later on when you are passing through, it's difficult to say what caused the destruction, unless something was burned down of course. I noted down another example, the date again is the 25th of July, but I cannot see the number -- 02081901. It's not far behind the previous one. If it is the 25th of July, 2001, you see a cornfield here and a house destroyed in the middle of it, and you see another two houses, one of them new and another one old, but still has a roof. It's a bit odd that in such a small area, if an army indeed had passed through, one house would be destroyed and the others would be left intact. I have seen such examples several times. 0281906, that's number 24, 25th of July, 2001 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may give one short comment. I don't think, but of course I would have to discuss it with my colleagues, that the Judges would consider when there's a roof on a house that it has -- perhaps it has been repaired over the last ten years since destruction took place, if the destruction took place in 1992. So therefore, it's good that you draw our attention to it that if that roof would be the roof that had been there for all those times, that you, at least, considered it odd that only one house is destroyed and not the other one, which of course is based already on quite a few conclusions, which the Chamber would not easily draw without further evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to deny anything, and I don't know who destroyed this in the first place. I'm not saying it wasn't the Serbs. I was just trying to work it out because I, myself, come from similar area -- from similar areas, similar lands. The other examples are similar, so I don't want to repeat myself. This one 02081906, it's curious the way the photographer took this shot. He cut a house that is intact down by the middle in order to show more houses that are destroyed. You see several houses under roofs and some covered by some sort of shrubbery. What I'm trying to say is that the person who took these pictures was trying to help and he wasn't perhaps too objective. He only wanted to show the bad things, while not showing examples that would speak to the opposite, that could help comparison. You see some settlements that are intact, roofs are intact, others are completely destroyed, you have both kinds of examples in this material. And I cannot deny that these things do not exist, but I wanted to say that it's difficult to perform expertise on the ground as to what happened exactly, when. You see a house that is intact and you don't know whether it was built after the war or before the war and then was simply not completed and not furnished. Those would be my general remarks, although I have reviewed every photograph one by one, and I do have certain comments but they would be arbitrary after all because I am not informed about what happened here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, just to -- Mr. Krajisnik, on the basis of these photographs, the Chamber will not establish that this destruction was -- what the Chamber wanted to get is a visual impression of what it meant. And as you are aware of, the Chamber also invited the Defence -- for example, if you see a village from an aerial photograph where half of them, the houses, are destroyed, that gives some kind of an impression. Of course, to say that if -- the kind of destruction makes it more or less probable that this was destruction caused by violence rather than any other means. And of course it -- it could well have been that the whole of the village had been destroyed or it could also mean that from one or two or three houses, that's general human experience, that the roofs have been taken off for repair. That's all possible. So -- but it gives some kind of impression, visual impression I would say, on what we -- on the kind of things we heard during the testimony of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you allow me, just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not gone to Zabrdje where my house is. Mr. Stewart travelled there. It was on Serb territory. However, a shell or two fell on the house and rains compounded the damage. What I'm trying to say is that if it's not lived in, the house deteriorates on its own; that's what my investigators told me at least. The house was not deliberately destroyed; it was just degraded by lack of use. And later, refugees stripped it of windows, doors, and took everything away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it -- if it would have presented to the Chamber that the Chamber would have received such information as how houses deteriorated as a consequence of the war, we certainly would have considered to receive those photographs and look at it as well, Mr. Krajisnik. There's hardly any doubt --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can bring you photographs. I believe Mr. Stewart has been there, and maybe he took some photos. Maybe he can tell you, because I was in The Hague at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where I said, I hardly could imagine that the Chamber would deny the presentation of such material, that's now for sure. If such material exists and if you would like to bring it to the attention of the Chamber, we'll certainly look at it, Mr. Krajisnik, for the same purposes; that is, to get a visual impression of what this war caused. Then I think it's time that we -- unless there's any other comment on this material. Then I'd like to continue the -- putting questions to you, Mr. Krajisnik. And let me just see whether I can find my way through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can skip over a couple of those questions and then continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to go a bit back to a question I put to you yesterday about the appointment of judges, which now I'm -- if you would please allow me to look exactly what you said yesterday. One second, please. Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, when I asked you yesterday about the appointment of the judiciary, you said the following. When I -- when you said that it was even a bigger problem, the problem of not having enough qualified judges, it became even a bigger problem when the Assembly refused to approve certain appointments, and there was no replacement available or when a judge left of his own accord. Would you have preferred that more judges would then have been confirmed by the Assembly than the Assembly actually did?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have thought this over last night, and if you want me to, I can tell you the whole story about those judges because I reviewed all the available material about the sessions where it was discussed, the conclusions, the whole issue of judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd first like you to answer my question. You said yesterday that the problem was even a bigger problem because the Assembly refused to approve certain appointments, and there was no replacement available. My question was whether you would have preferred that more appointments would have been confirmed by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said yesterday I stand by. It would have been better if the Assembly had approved all the nominations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was whether you would have preferred that; whether it's better or not is an objective assessment. I'm asking whether you would have preferred that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have preferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I also asked you did you raise your voice when the Assembly refused to approve certain appointments? And you answered: "Well, we did have a consultative meeting about these appointments," and I'm quoting from page 26.103, "and we were quite satisfied because you cannot come across as a democratic state in the eyes of the international community if your own people are against judges simply because they belong to a different ethnic community. But the atmosphere was such that the MPs were convinced that it was up to them to decide. So when it came to a vote, they got their way. What I could do and what I did do as the Speaker, I tried to organise discussions in such a way as to protect these nominations because it was politically wise and also fair in the humane sense. It was very politically unhelpful, to say the least." This suggests, Mr. Krajisnik, that as far as you're concerned that you're unhappy that the Assembly did not confirm all of the proposals put to it -- or as a matter of fact, these were appointments that needed confirmation, and that you were unhappy that the Assembly did not approve them. Is that a correct understanding of that answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that I said yesterday, as you have just repeated it is true, and I'll explain why, although the transcript says something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript of what? Of this court or the transcript of --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of that session of the Assembly. The transcript of that Assembly session can give a different impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then tell us, first of all, what you actually, as the president of the Assembly, did in relation to this. What positions did you take, did you express any -- any view of being unhappy with confirmations to be denied, or could you explain to us what you did in a factual way, please. So not theories, but what happened, what you did, what the others did. Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did what is recorded in the transcript. I put it up for a vote to see who was against, who was for, and all the Yugoslavs, Montenegrins, and Muslims did not pass. And Serbs, with some exceptions, did pass. And I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm still asking you -- so you're now describing that it was put to a vote. My question comprised also what you did, apart from putting it to a vote. Did you give support to the appointments? Did you -- what was your role, if any, apart from putting it to a vote?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I played the most positive part from the very beginning, and I can explain that. But if you are -- if you talk only about the 18th of August, you cannot understand it. Well, I am saying it was positive, and I can explain that, if you are interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- yes. First tell us what you did, and then the assessment on whether and why it was positive, we'll look at that later. What you said your role, apart from putting it to a vote.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will get a wrong picture, Mr. President. I want to tell you nicely how it all went from the beginning to end, and you are looking just at the conclusion from the last session. I know exactly what's written there, and I know what you read and what confuses you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it confuses me or not is still to be seen. But I would like you to --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must be confused, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My first question to you is: What did you do during that session. And then I'll give you an opportunity to explain. But I'd first like to focus on what happened.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I did. The session was held on the 11th of August, and the nominations of judges from Banja Luka was not discussed there. I told you -- in fact, I told them, all the items that you are not ready to discuss today, put them on the agenda tomorrow, on the 12th of August. And on the 12th of August they brought this list that was not harmonised. It was not finalised. Some were against, some were for. And at the meeting of the Deputies' Club I realised they wanted to get Muslims -- Muslims, Montenegrins and Yugoslavs off the list. And from the 25th of July, I knew that the situation had not matured, had not ripened, because the issue of citizenship was not resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I was clear. I want -- when the matter was put to a vote, we're talking about the Banja Luka judges, I want to know what you said and what you did during that Assembly meeting. Later, if there's any need to hear that, we'll hear about what happened during the Deputies' Club meeting, of which we have no minutes. But first I'd like to see what happened on this Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the session itself, the minister came to the rostrum and said there is a harmonised list of judges to be appointed. I have the list with me. Do you want to go through the names one by one? So that's what we did. Some names were taken off the list and others were left there. The ones that were taken off were mainly Muslims, Croats, Montenegrins, and Yugoslavs, so what you read is true, is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was -- what did you do? That was also part of my question, not only what the minister did, and apart from putting it to a vote, whether you intervened in the debate and what did you say about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did intervene -- I did intervene when Mr. Karadzic said: Why are we taking Muslims, Croats, and Yugoslavs off the list? And I answered: We are not taking them off the list because they are Yugoslavs, Muslims, and Montenegrins, it's just that we're not filling those vacancies right now. We can prepare them for a vote tomorrow, because there was a problem around it. And those who were proposing them quarrelled among themselves; that's in the transcript. There was an objection when a Serb was taken off the list because some people were saying he was communist, others said he wasn't. I know every single thing I did at that session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then what happened then on the next day -- so do I understand that you say -- you explained to Mr. Karadzic that you are not taking Muslims, Croats, and Yugoslavs off the list because they are Muslims, Croats, and Montenegrins, but you are just not confirming their appointment, that's how I understand, filling those vacancies, or --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, no. They were not voted for, but the vacancies were not filled. There were no other judges who were appointed, so then we could prepare for the next session. You know what the atmosphere was like? It could have gone on for a hundred years that session, and no appointments would have come through. It's all in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the next day, what happened the next day, that's, I take it, the 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This was on the 12th. And did you then -- so you would say it was not that whether they were taken off the list or was their appointment not confirmed? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vacancies just remained. In order to overcome the problem on that particular day, that is. I wanted this to get through as if it were just judges and that there was nothing else involved, and then the next day, say, you could have appointed other judges. But others didn't understand that and then they kept insisting: Well, he's a Yugoslav but he's good; and he's a Montenegrin, but he's good, and so on and so forth. And that turned out to be a problem, and nothing went through. And I can tell you why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th of June, on the 3rd of July, and on the 15th of July, we had a consultative meeting. I have it here. Many judges were appointed there at the proposal of the minister and of the grassroots, Muslims, Croats, Serbs, Montenegrins, everybody. I was there at the meeting, and you have that session there that is called the Presidency. Karadzic signed it, and this was published in the Official Gazette. On the 27th of July, when that session was held on the 25th and the 27th, a man came from Konjic. He said that there were 3.500 Serb civilians imprisoned in Celibici. A high representative of the SDS spoke then and said: I see this list. I see Muslim judges here. They are drinking coffee up there in Bijeljina, whereas other people are getting killed and our people are in prison. And that caused the mayhem. The Muslims stayed there, but when they came to take the solemn oath, they didn't take the solemn oath. You will see that Milan Novakovic says on the 12th of August that they could not take the solemn oath. On the 12th of August, we got this unprepared material from Banja Luka, and that was when we were discussing the proposal of the Vance-Owen Plan. The MPs were so bitter because Republika Srpska was being done away with, and I realised that nothing would get through because the conclusion of the 27th of July was -- well, that's what lawyers said anyway, that a law on citizenship had to be passed and that only citizens of Republika Srpska could be appointed judges. We were in a hurry then in order to get to the meeting in London, and then on the 12th we had a discussion about this proposal, which was disastrous. The MPs were so angry at the Montenegrins and at the Serbs from Serbia and the Yugoslavs and everybody else. So the climate simply wasn't right for this to get through. And I quite simply said: Well, wait a minute, let's go ahead as if there were no one there. Let us adopt a list of 50 judges, but let's not handle it in this atmosphere. In this atmosphere we could have gone on for years and years, and we wouldn't have finished this. It says there was an attack on Pale as well. I didn't want the session to go on for three days. I wanted to go back to Pale because my family was there. I wasn't the only one. That was the situation that we are all facing. That is the actual truth. If I wanted to be against Muslims or Croats, I would have been against them on the 20th of June, the 3rd of July. I would have said to Karadzic: Why are you making this proposal? But I was at this consultative meeting, and all these people were proposed, and this was very important for us politically, in addition to the fact that this was a humane thing. If somebody was a good judge, there is no reason hat they should be discriminated against. I was looking through all this until this morning, and I knew that something happened, and then I remembered what it was all about. And you've got it all in the documents here, too. You know what Karadzic said out there? He said: Gentlemen, Alija is paying Serbs with gold so that he would have them there, whereas look at what you're doing. But they said: No, no, and they got rid of the Montenegrins, the Yugoslavs, the Muslims, everybody, so what could I do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did Mr. Karadzic say in respect of these judges to be appointed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have to apologise I got so carried away. I'm saying that what was indicated then was the fact that it was not good for us to turn down other ethnic groups, but believe me everybody considered Montenegrins to be Serbs and they didn't want them either. And then communists? No. If somebody was a Serb but a communist, a former communist, no way. The atmosphere was so electrified. So then I said: Well, you know, let's try to prepare this tomorrow when the climate is better. That's the whole story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you talking about tomorrow or about half a year later or a year later?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Figuratively, figuratively. It could be in five days. The Presidency could also send this list of people out apart from the Assembly or say to the next Assembly, but once the atmosphere was a bit different. We also discussed the platform there for London, you'll see, the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was the atmosphere in the Assembly rather than war situation that would guide you in not appointing or confirming the appointment of Muslim, Croat, Montenegrin judges. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not being confirmed, Your Honour. New ones were being elected, new ones in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the role of the Assembly was to confirm appointments, new appointments?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, no. What I was telling you about, the 20th of June, the 3rd of July. This, on the other hand, was the 27th of July, whereas this was the 12th of August, Banja Luka, new ones brought to the Assembly, and no one had agreed on that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's see what happens -- by the way, you're very much blaming the atmosphere created by the Assembly members that you could not make these appointments. Let me then perhaps repeat my last question but in a slightly different way. Was it the atmosphere in the Assembly at that time or was it that in a war situation you would consider it not a good idea to appoint Muslim judges, Croat judges? I mean, you very much emphasised that the Assembly members -- the atmosphere would change in one or two or three, five days, and then everything would be possible. Is it -- therefore, is it the atmosphere created by the Assembly members that guided you in not promoting or not further promoting the appointment of these Muslim, Croat, and Montenegrin judges in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of August, I did not want to insist on something that could not be carried through only due to the atmosphere. Was I opposed to it? I would have been opposed to it on the 20th of June, the 3rd of July, and so on. I would have said: What do we need Muslims for? But this simply could not get through. It had not prepared sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not an answer to my question. My question was -- you said: I did not want to insist. Was it because of the atmosphere created by the Assembly members, or was there any other reason that led you not to insist -- or even not to encourage the appointment of judges of non-Serb nationality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew that it could not be carried through, because there was this conclusion reached on the 27th of July, the proposal of Milojevic. I also knew that it could not be carried through the club, and I found this Solomonic solution. He had given a different proposal, not to fill the vacancies -- or rather, to move on as if there was no ethnicity involved. Let us try to appoint whoever we can, and then when the right atmosphere is created, let us try to appoint whoever. I didn't know about any one of the names. I didn't know who had proposed them. Later on during the war -- you're absolutely right. The further the war went, there were more opponents to having Muslims and Croats appointed to such positions, but it wasn't that way at that moment, it was just a momentary thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Momentary thing caused by the Assembly members?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. I mean, I don't want all of this to be taken so literally. On the 27th of July, when we went to the London Conference and when we brought back this material that did not suit the MPs, that was the atmosphere where they felt so bitter, because they realised there was no Republika Srpska. And they blamed everybody, the international community, the Muslims and the Croats, and the Yugoslavia that voted, Montenegro that voted. Everybody was being blamed. So now at that moment you bring in this unprepared material and there are people from Banja Luka who are in favour of it and people from Banja Luka who are opposed to that. All of that is in the record, and I know exactly what it is like. And then presidents of courts came out and spoke and besieged them. I know what the atmosphere was like, and I know every particular MP and I know exactly how they reacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have given it a chance to have them all appointed as proposed, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely would have, like on the 20th of June, absolutely, because I think it was a great pity for you not to take these people in. I mean, really. I know what it was like politically speaking, and then in addition to that you don't have experts. A judge has to be a professional. What am I supposed to say now? There are no Serbs and I am being tried? No. You have to have professionals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if the atmosphere among the Assemblymen would not have been so much against it, then you would have seen no problems in appointing them all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have said: Well, let's adopt the whole list, the whole list. Believe me, that is what I would have said, because I was in a hurry. You have a list, who is for, who is against, that's it. But they said: Well, let's move along individually so that we could have at least some appointments. The courts could not operate. They had no judges, and it was the month of August and there were no judges. I see no reason why these people could not be appointed to these positions in Republika Srpska to this day. And they can do their work. They can conduct trials, they can do whatever they're supposed to do. I see no reason why that could not be done. That is what we said in our discussion on the 20th of June, when Karadzic said: Let us not be against this, we should have it wherever possible, and that's what we did -- or rather, that's what he did. But I was there at that meeting, and on the 3rd of July and on the 15th of July, and so on and so forth, and it was published in the Official Gazette, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you support Mr. Karadzic when he was expressing himself in favour of multi-ethnic appointments in the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of August, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not support him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not support him. Why didn't you support him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because he pointed out something that was really wrong. Let's go through this here -- I mean, he could have appointed them five days later without the Assembly had he not pointed that out as the problems of Muslims and Croats. And when you bring that to the fore, then they're going to say: Why did you make these appointments when we were opposed to it? I didn't want that to be seen, Muslims, Croats, whatever. I simply wanted to have a vote on judges. He somehow pointed this out, other MPs did, too, and, quite simply, it became obvious, whereas I wanted us to go through all these proposals. And after all, you adopt the whole list, and then the next day the Presidency could adopt it and make it public. And then there would be a Assembly with a better atmosphere, but he did not understand me when I was saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your suggestion, more or less, was: Let's do it silently, let's do it in such a way, it will be done within a week, and then we have them all appointed, and there's no problem, and it would not arise any further discussion and debate. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the whole truth. I knew that that proposal, the way it was, could not come through. It was not prepared and there were great antagonisms involved. People were bitter for other reasons. I didn't want to have a debate on this, who was a Serb, a Croat, or a Muslim. I wanted to move down the list, who was in favour, who was against, and that ultimately we adopt a certain number. These other people, because there were these vacancies, could be discussed at a different session when the atmosphere is better or the Presidency could appoint them. But if they're being discussed as Muslims, Croats, Yugoslavs, whatever, no. But then when you look at them as judges only. When they realise that, then it turned in to be a problem. They said: Ah, we appointed a Muslim in Bijeljina, he didn't even come to take the solemn oath. There was a war going on. They thought that they were our enemies. I mean, really. There was a proposal involving a man when they said: He is not a Croat, his mother is a Serb. It is such a problem when you start discussing these things that are so bad and unpopular. The whole proposal was unprepared. It was presented by the president of the Banja Luka municipality instead of the chairman of some appointments commission or something, because this is a pretty big area. That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You now introduced the circumstance that it was a war time. Would that mean for you that during such a war judges of a different nationality should not or it would not be wise to appoint them during a war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was mentioned very often because people did not feel right. Those who were on trial, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking what others thought. My question was: Would that mean for you, so what was your opinion about that, whether you should or you should not or whether it would not be wise to appoint judges of another ethnicity in this wartime.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that it wasn't wise. I know what you're reading now. But I was in favour of these appointments on the 20th of June, on the 3rd of July, and so on and so forth. I wanted them to be there because we needed that. Look it up and you'll see. There were many people who were appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have a look at what happened. Could you please look -- I -- we have a B/C/S version of --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got all of it right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P583, tab 87, copies are available. Yes. Page 10 in the B/C/S, page 11 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could we please have a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have -- in the B/C/S, I have it on page 10, but do we have copies? I tried to distribute everything. And it's page 11 out of 82 in English. Do you have copies?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We haven't received any copies and we need to know what session it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's the 19th Session of the Assembly, 12th of August, 1992, in Banja Luka. Mr. Krajisnik, when you opened the debate, you said: "I hereby open a separate debate on every judge separately." Then the following passage, that is still you who is speaking where it says: "1. Vesna Antonic: I would only like to reiterate." Is that you who is speaking?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. All of that is me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's slowly go through it. You said: "I would only like to reiterate the conclusions from a session in Pale, when we discussed the appointment of judges to the lower court in Bijeljina. At that time Mr. Milojevic gave an acceptable explanation that we should not appoint judges of different nationality until the issue is resolved, that this will be a state of Serbs and other citizens, while the rights of the citizens and the positions to which they can be appointed would be decided later on. Therefore," you said, "I believe, if we have reached such conclusions in Pale, we could then delay the appointment of judges until a constitution precisely defines which positions citizens of other nationalities can occupy. Mr. Milojevic, the person who gave the explanation, could define that better than me. Perhaps even here we should proceed in this manner and appoint only the proposed Serb judges, while the Croat and Muslim candidates would be appointed only by the constitution, which we're definitely going to change, ensures such rights for them." This was more or less your opening remark on the matter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't this an opening remark that clearly disencourages the appointment of any other judges than those of Serb nationality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. I'm telling you. I knew exactly that they wanted to reject the whole list of judges. I wanted this to be carried through. That's what they were saying at the club, that they wanted -- they concluded that they would actually reject everything, but I wanted at least something to be adopted. And the constitution was changed at this session -- or rather, one of these sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just explained a couple of minutes ago that it was just a matter of change of the atmosphere created by the Assemblymen, and that after five days, you said, or just soon after that there would be -- you could just fill the vacancies and then the matter would be resolved. Here you suggest that you would need to change the constitution to reach such new appointments. I see some contradiction in what you just said and what I just read. Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no contradiction, none whatsoever. I am trying to forestall things because Mr. Milojevic said all of that and then there was the conclusion, too. I wanted to forestall things. And you will see later on what the discussion was like. If I allow them to continue the discussion, it could have gone on for three days and nothing could have happened. I mean, if you want to believe differently, I cannot convince you otherwise. Look at the discussions and you will see what it's like. Look at the 27th of July, too. It's not my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is because the Assembly members, the atmosphere was such that they would not want to appoint any Muslim, any Croat, any Montenegrin. Is that a correct understanding? That in that atmosphere you would have lost the whole of the list?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. We were the Deputies' Club, I know that exactly, and people were first opposed to it. You have it here who made the proposals and who said who was a communist and how did they have the right to do this and that. There were hundreds of objections in addition to who's a Muslim, who's a Croat. They wanted to reject the whole list. The president of the court is asking them: Please, appoint at least this one man. I wanted to forestall that kind of conclusion. They knew about it. It was there ten days ago on the 27th of July. You will see what the discussion was like, and you will see later who said what and who persecuted Serbs and what have you not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you started the vote and you said: "Thank you very much." That's on page 13, both of the English and the B/C/S. "We're going to take a vote on each one and you should bear everything in mind. For your reference I'm going to read out everyone's name, surname, father's name, and nationality." Why was it necessary to read the father's name? Is that because that's usually done?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, I have no way of explaining this to you. I have no way of explaining to you that the way you are drawing conclusions is wrong. I have told you exactly what I wanted to do and what this was all about. You will find it here what I said after Slobodanka Hrvacanin spoke. If you wanted to conclude that I was against Muslims, then why did I support them on the 12th -- on the 20th of June? I simply cannot convince you, I cannot persuade you, I cannot. I can go on explaining for five years and it's no use. I mean, if you want to conclude something, then what can I do about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no conclusions in my mind. I'm trying to establish at this moment facts, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, the facts are here, and I know all of that. I'm telling you, three times before that we discussed this. I knew who was a Muslim and who was a Croat, and so on and so forth. And all of this was made public, and the situation was the way it was. And now when we're taking things out of context, there is no way for me to explain it. If you want to make a different conclusion, then what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you please answer my questions and refrain from --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make one observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik in the answer before last said: "You will find it here, what I said after Slobodanka Hrvacanin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With just a little bit of respect, Your Honour, I suggest that when Mr. Krajisnik says that, it might be helpful to look at the passage he plainly is referring to a section of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if he has a specific part in mind. I don't know whether it's among the portion --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that's the question really, Your Honour, whether he does, in which case perhaps Your Honour might just give him the opportunity if he does have a specific thing in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if he can do that precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's was my request, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- the problem is, Mr. Krajisnik, that I copied those portions of the session on which I would like to ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He speaks on page 23, Your Honour, if it's possible, without my leading too directly. It is possible that that is the bit he has in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, we'll come to that. We'll come to later discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll certainly come to other parts of it. Mr. Krajisnik, if you would look at number 8 on the list on who was voted which is Dusanka Fazlic. The --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The minutes read that there was laughter. Could you explain why there was laughter, when I take it you have read Dusanka Fazlic, a Serb daughter of Avdo.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here lies the answer as to what I tried to explain about what kind of atmosphere prevailed. People were simply against all those nominees, and I told them to get serious, stop laughing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But why was there laughing? I mean, laughing appears only on number 8 and not on any of the other numbers.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because her father is a Fazlic, which means Muslim, and she is a Serb. That's why they were laughing because she was a daughter of an Avdo, and Avdo is a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a mixed marriage, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's then clear to me why there was laughter there. Then -- well, then we see that we go through the first 11. I move on now, and we then have on page 16, on page 17, and on page 18 we have many other names. And the general impression is that Serbs are usually elected, other nationalities usually not. Most of the times the names --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therein lies my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the times the name of the father is mentioned, not always. And you just explained to us that the name of the father, being Avdo, on number 8 gave a clue as to the Muslim origin of the father. Now, I move to page 18, both of the B/C/S and the English. There Dr. Karadzic says, after you've dealt with number 29: "I need to say something, not only about this proposal but about the principle of the matter, if I may. Look, as we said yesterday we have to determine if he or she is appropriate, but as far as other nations are concerned we have a percentage, a proportion participating in the municipal authorities. We have to be responsible, as we are creating a state. You are the organ creating it. The state must be created swiftly and in the best way. The state must have all its elements in order to survive and remain as a state. I can't elaborate on this longer, but I know what I'm saying. Believe me, Alija pays fortune to any Serb willing to stay and work on his territory. He begs the metropolitan bishop there and sends his people to convince him. I think that the Serbian people know how to make a state, and because we know how to make a state we need to make it with all elements." Then in the transcript you intervene, Mr. Krajisnik, and you say the following: "Radovan, let me explain. Nobody rejects because they are not good or because they are Muslims or Croats. Simply, we have decided to declare ourselves now because we are in the state of a civil war. So they will lose this number of judges, and when the war is over they will be re-elected." I would have two questions to you, Mr. Krajisnik. At that time did you expect either the constitution to be changed within a couple of days or did you consider the war to be over in a couple of days?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that the atmosphere, the prevails sentiment, would change in just a few days and those people could then be elected without any problem. Just as the first batch was elected, they could be elected, too. I didn't think about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you please answer my question. We have now seen three reasons for -- possible reasons for not appointing non-Serb judges at that time. You gave -- before we looked at these texts, you said it was the atmosphere created by the Assembly members mainly that made clear to you that nothing would come through. Then in the beginning, let me call it your opening statement, you said: There is a constitutional problem, we have to change the constitution before we can appoint. And now in the midst of the discussion you explained to Mr. Karadzic that the non-Serbs will lose the number of judges and that when the war is over -- so I'm focussing only on the last two, where you said before that the way would be free to appoint them in a couple of days, I think you mentioned five but -- well, soon, very soon. So my question now is not whether the atmosphere would change but whether you would consider the constitution to have been changed within a couple of days or the war to be over in a couple of days. So focussing on these two possible reasons for not appointing the non-Serb judges at that time. We'll come to the -- no, no --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just a question of atmosphere. Only a question of atmosphere that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll come to the atmosphere later, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm just asking you at this moment whether you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought the prevailing sentiment would change in just a few days, and then they would be able to be elected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, now for the third time you seem to refuse to answer my question. Of course I do understand that you thought that the atmosphere would change quickly, but since you gave two other elements which would make it unwise or even impossible, that is the constitution and the state of a civil war; I'm asking you since you said: After a couple of days everything would be fine, whether you expected either the constitution to be changed within a couple of days or the war to be over in a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's move on. We got a --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just say this one thing, Mr. President? Here Karadzic made his statement here and there was a vote later. Look at the vote. Karadzic presented it all to them -- if you think it's I who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- no, we'll come to the vote. We'll go through it slowly, step by step. Then on page 21, spilling over to 22, of the English, and it might be 20 to 21 in the B/C/S, after number 47, we see that a discussion develops on Rada Sumbo, where people are starting -- making remarks on the qualities of that person, some saying that -- that they wouldn't know what she had done as a judge; others claiming that this lady while she was the president of the court in Jajce employed mostly Muslims in the court and that no Serbian judges could have any influence. So there starts a debate on the qualities of this lady, including her previous behaviour in relation to non-Serb judges in the court of Jajce. Is that -- do we agree that that's what happens then, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. Do you mean whether what is written here is correct? I don't remember. But since it's written there, it must be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm summarising what it says, and I just wanted to find out whether you agree with the summary I just gave so that we are talking on the same --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I wasn't following you. I was kind of reading through, and I didn't quite understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you agree that such a discussion here started and then a vote was taken on Rada Sumbo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the deputy Prime Minister for justice intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, with different views on -- different appreciations of that person. Then -- by the way, she is then not elected. Then we have a few more. And then we come to Milorad Krkeljas, who is Serb. And then Slobodanka Hrvacanin expresses that she was unpleasantly surprised by the proposal of Mr. Krkeljas. This is the portion, I take it, that you wanted to refer. This is where Mrs. Hrvacanin speaks.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she says she would rather vote for any Muslim than for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and why doesn't she want to vote for him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do I know? She lived in Zenica where he was a judge, and she must have had something against him. I don't know who he is in the first place and what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but my question was why Ms. Hrvacanin was opposed to him. She expressed that, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she said here that he was in favour of Muslims, that he had distanced himself from Serbs and the SDS, that he wasn't a patriot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the way he approached Serbs in the SDS was part of the appreciation of this person. Then you intervened, Mr. Krajisnik. I have no specific questions about it, but if you want to explain further on your intervention I will give you an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, this was proposed by the president of the municipality of Banja Luka, because she asks who nominated this man. And I didn't want to root for a Serb to be elected. I used the same phrase in both those cases, who's for, who's against. And I added, I believe, Slobodanka and everything she says, but I believe it is in principle wrong to pursue staffing policy like this. It's ugly the way we are voting about judges. Something is wrong with these proposals from Jajce and Zenica. It's nominated by our man from Banja Luka, and we are all against in a high degree. I feel like abstaining in each one of those cases. I feel like abstaining on each one of these proposals, but it's true, we have the right to be for or against. However, if these proposals that were rejected, if they are later substantiated, there is still room for them because this is just voting without any arguing. I note that we did not appoint Milorad Krkeljas judge of a Banja Luka court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So you expressed your unhappiness with what happened at that time and with the procedure that was followed. Then the next is about deputy prosecutors, number 1 to 11, and then judges of the high court in Banja Luka, which goes on for the next few pages. And then you come to -- at page 27 in the English, I think it's also page 27 of the B/C/S, we come to the high court judges. And a discussion starts when the appointment of Mr. Gojko Vukotic is discussed. I then see that a certain Jovo Rosic takes the floor. And there is some discussion on this person who is of Montenegrin or who declared himself as Montenegrin. There is a discussion which goes to explain why he -- whether he really was a Montenegrin, yes or no, and who made him declare himself a Montenegrin. And then in earlier days he declared himself as a Serb. When he was to be appointed in his previous position they needed a Croat; the president of the court told him to declare himself as a Croat. Please, it's up to you now, says Jovo Rosic. Then you put this to a vote. It reads, and I'm now on -- still on page 27: "Gojko Vukotic, a Montenegrin. Does anyone want to take part in the discussion? No. Who is in favour? 31. Who is against? 5. Who is abstaining? 7." And then you say: "The proposal did not pass because it required a 50 per cent-plus majority of votes in favour." And then you say: "Let's establish a quorum with regard to the Tosic case." Mr. Krajisnik, could you explain to me how this functioned that 31 votes in favour, 5 against, and seven abstentions would not meet the threshold of a 50 per cent-plus majority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our constitution and in the rules of procedure, out of 83 MPs there has to be a majority of 42 in favour of every decision; that is to say, 50-plus majority in terms of the entire number of MPs, not only of MPs present. That is why the situation was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you say -- so that was the reason why this vote was in -- well, just Mr. Vukotic didn't pass because there were no 43 votes. Okay. Now on the next page it says: "There are 60 of us present. Shall we vote again? Here is Petko Cancar to explain about Vukotic." What was the reason 60 Assembly members being present, the 43 votes not reached -- I noted for myself that 31 is a 50-plus situation if there are 60 present; it is not 43. As a matter of fact, there were 43 members that voted or abstained. Why should one vote again? I mean, what was the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You see, Mr. President, there has to be a quorum at every session. Out of 83, 42 represent a quorum. There have to be 42 people there in order for the Assembly to work. We had 60 MPs. We had a quorum. However, when the MPs voted, not all of them voted. 31 voted, 38 -- 43. Then I established that either there was not a quorum or not everybody voted, and that is why the vote was supposed to be taken again. Then Mr. Cancar took the floor to support Vukotic once again so that he would be elected because he knew him. In our Assembly, there had to be 42 deputies for every decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So Mr. Cancar was very much in favour. He called Mr. Vukotic. He said -- he called him more or less one of the best judges -- "I'm just saying that Gojko Vukotic is an excellent judge. We lawyers have admired his sentences. I think that many of his sentences will be historical." So I've hardly ever seen a greater praise for a candidate as we see it here. Then you intervened, Mr. Krajisnik. You say: "Please, we didn't reject this. If we haven't elected someone, there are still vacancies. Any proposition can be re-evaluated. The climate can be changed, and they can be elected at the end. Now, those who got more than half of the votes will be elected." And then after Mr. Kupresanin has been speaking, you again take the floor and say: "Let me explain this a bit. If we don't declare ourselves the deputies, we are discussing the qualities of judges. The current political situation is like that. It is not clear, and therefore we are taking some issues off the agenda. We are not appointing other people. We are discussing the qualities and whether certain people could be elected. The ones not being elected could be reconsidered in the coming period, proposed again, and elected. Therefore, this is not discrimination against the person that we are taking off now." And then you say: "Let's go on. We are voting again because we have established that not everyone has voted. Who is in favour? 16 are in favour. Who is against? 19 are against. Did anyone abstain? The rest abstained." Do you have any explanation or did you ever hear from those who changed their vote why, after such a -- as it's said in Latin, such a laudatio, why Mr. Cancar was expressed and once you had emphasised, very strongly, two times that if you wouldn't elect someone today you could still elect him tomorrow, why 15 of the Assembly members were not voting in favour of Mr. Vukotic anymore. Did you ever hear anything from those who voted what made them change their mind?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody had a reason why they vote against, but I heard the reason why they were opposed to Montenegrins. At the conference in London, Montenegro allegedly supported these Vance-Owen principles, whatever, and now the MPs were angry at Montenegrins. That was the whole philosophy involved. Had there been somebody there who was a Serb from Serbia, they would have been against him too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this awareness came up for 15 of those who had voted in favour of Mr. Vukotic within five minutes, because 31 voted in favour of him, and in the second round only 16. Do I have to understand that a sudden awareness of the positions of Montenegrins, of whom only good words were spoken in the meantime, that that sudden awareness would explain the difference of 15 Assembly members who were not in favour anymore of Mr. Vukotic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No awareness. They were against the Montenegrins from the start, but then there are people who changed their positions depending on the vote. I cannot know why somebody votes in favour now and then later on votes against. If they take the vote 15 times, they change their position every time. Some people are like that. Oh, you mean this discussion affected these people? Oh, no way. Believe me, nothing. Karadzic, Rosic, and the rest, the majority were always against. I knew that there couldn't be 42 in favour. This man happened to be a Montenegrin, and he was elected after some time. I don't remember how much later. He's an excellent judge, but he wasn't appointed then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where you say they were against the Montenegrins from the start, that at least in the previous round of voting seems not to have been the case where it was 31 in favour, 5 against, and 7 abstentions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, are you trying to say that now there were less? Well, how can I know why the number went from 31 to 16. I have no idea. Oh, it was Kupresanin, Kupresanin who had an influence. His discussion was negative. That is why the number went down, I think. A partial communist, that's what he said, and that affected people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said: I could have no idea. Is it -- did anyone explain to you why they changed their votes? That's what I asked. That's just a fact whether anyone told you not to guess about it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. This is --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Specifically I didn't hear from anyone. I was just talking about Montenegrins in general, and this was really such a surprise that they were so opposed to Montenegrins. But that's the way it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the clock. We have a break now. I will move to another subject after the break. So this, as far as I'm concerned, closes the questions on appointment of judges. We'll have a break to 25 minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, a few more questions. One of the issues we have not spent much attention on was the establishment of a company called Novi Privrednik. You remember that it -- that it was established?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you tell us more about that company. What was its purpose exactly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novi Privrednik, well, the idea came from people who lived in Sarajevo and who remember Privrednik from the days of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. That was a Serb company that financed the schooling of children, students, and was involved in humanitarian work. When the Serb Democratic Party came to power, it advocated privatisation, and a drive was launched to establish Novi Privrednik, a new Privrednik, a company that would involve a large number of people, everyone who wanted to be part of this. It was stated here that Mr. Trbojevic carried out the registration on instructions from Mr. Karadzic. People were supposed to invest some monies so that it would get going, this company. In actual fact, I don't know whether it actually did start working. I think it did for a month or two. It was supposed to avail itself of a particular economic situation; namely, that there was a shortage of many goods in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that could have been imported from Serbia, especially food. In this way the shareholders -- or should I call them the members of this company, in fact imported goods through Novi Privrednik and made some money in the process. In the meantime, since Novi Privrednik was not actually in operation, this role was taken over in part by Boksit Milici that had its office in the Holiday Inn until Novi Privrednik started operating. The Executive Board of the Serb Democratic Party took care of Novi Privrednik, organised its assembly, and the company was supposed to get organs of its own and start operating finally. That would be it, in the briefest possible terms, about Novi Privrednik. There was no major effect and the war soon broke out, and I think that it dwindled away on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was the role of the SDS exactly in creating such a company in which I do understand to import goods and to make some money out of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the role of the SDS was to promote the idea among its own members so that people would join Novi Privrednik at regional levels, too. Later on it was left to its own shareholders' assembly and other organs. One thing is for sure and that is that the Serb Democratic Party did not have any true sources of income, and it probably expected to get some resources through donations once Novi Privrednik earned a profit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you yourself play any role in Novi Privrednik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the preparatory work was concerned, I, together with Momcilo Pejic, minister of finance, and I don't know who else was there, played an active role in order to convey my own experience in this attempt to set up this company. Actually, it was hard to explain this to people, that now they were supposed to be shareholders of a company after socialism and to see whether they would earn a profit and so on. I mean, as far as organisation is concerned, in part, in the beginning I played a rather active role, but later on I didn't due to my commitments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say: "In the beginning I played a rather active role." What was that in time, in the beginning until when?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe -- how can I say? Well, perhaps a month, and later on when the assembly and the organs were supposed to be established I didn't take part in it. See, I remember that a meeting in Banja Luka was supposed to be attended in order to explain to people what the purpose of Novi Privrednik was. And I talked to Minister Pejic and asked him whether he could send someone there, since he was rather immobile, in order for somebody to explain the idea of Novi Privrednik to people out there. I think I had a few meetings. Later on -- I don't know if I took an active part in it. I don't think so. Later on, I do not think I took an active part in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you financially involved in Novi Privrednik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like all others, I was a shareholder, and my father was, my brother was, my relatives, and other people. I gave Novi Privrednik some shares -- or rather, I bought some shares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was the level of your being a shareholder the ordinary level or were you -- did you take a specific position in -- among the shareholders?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No. No one had a specific position. I did not play any role. As a matter of fact, as for Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic, I suggested to them that they should give some money, that they should become shareholders. But as for this part that you have as a shareholder, you could buy some goods for that part, and then through Novi Privrednik - how should I put this? - you could have it realised. It depended on the number of shares you bought. I didn't have a role in that company, not in its management, not in its assembly, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But were you a bigger shareholder or ordinary or small compared to other shareholders?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, compared to others I guess I was a bigger shareholder. I mean -- well, there was a bigger amount involved. I cannot remember now how this could be converted into present-day money, but yes, I guess I did have a bigger share than some others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And some others or most of the others?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that there were some other people who had the same amount that I did, but I cannot remember now. But I certainly did take part with a significant -- well, significant. Well, sort of a significant amount of money as a shareholder. There were a lot of shareholders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was Novi Privrednik just commercial in the sense that they would buy and sell goods to the public, or did they have any specific relationship with government, governmental organs in Republika Srpska? So I mean were they dealing just with private parties, or were they also -- was Novi Privrednik also involved in supplying goods for the army, the government -- well, whatever public organs there would have been?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I mean, at that time -- well, Republika Srpska was not actually functioning. I think that every shareholder was supposed to buy some goods and find a buyer. He could do that, but not, say, supply government institutions. It was still Bosnia-Herzegovina, so there weren't some Serb organs of government, if I can put it that way, that should have been - how should I put this? - provided for, supplied with goods. All of that was, say, until February, March 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a major shareholder, as you said, a more substantial shareholder, what goods did you buy for which you intended to find a buyer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not really involved in that. I know that my brother once asked before the new year: What are we going to do with this money? And he bought some light bulbs and he sold them to someone. It's the only business deal he carried through on his own behalf, on my behalf, and on our father's behalf. With this money, he bought some imported light bulbs and sold them somewhere. Well, that's what I remember. I don't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know to whom he sold it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I have no idea -- I mean, I don't remember. It could have been some company or whatever. I don't know. I think there were some imported light bulbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then it all stopped after the war had started, because you're talking about a couple of months of activity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, say, from November to February/March, not more than that, November 1991 until February, perhaps, 1992. Actually, I don't think it even operated for longer than a month because this includes both preparations and its actual work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Mr. Krajisnik, I move to another subject, which is a meeting which supposedly took place on the 2nd of September, 1992. We find that in a document, a document being a diary of Colonel Novica Simic. Do you remember that this document which was introduced through Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the meeting in Bijeljina, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, could -- does Your Honour have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- it should be -- let me just have a look. It is part of the Brown material, and I'm not very precise at this moment. I think it's tab 59 of the Brown material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I see Mr. Sladojevic is working on it straight away as we speak, so we'll -- thank you for that. We'll track that down, I'm quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would like -- and then we find that on pages 37 and 38. It describes a meeting, Mr. Krajisnik. It says: "Meeting with RS Presidency, the 2nd of September." Mr. Registrar, do we have the document here or not? A copy is printed out for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise. I would also like to draw your attention to the 27th Presidency Session -- as a matter of fact, 27A, as it is called, which is P65, 194. I apologise for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for not having the copy ready. Mr. Usher, would you -- because I'll then first concentrate on the 27th Session. Mr. Krajisnik, when we're looking at the minutes of the 27th Session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic on the 31st of August, 1992, I see that during that session Mr. Mladic and Mr. Gvero arrived during the meeting. We find that close to the end. It then reads: "The generals briefed the Presidency in detail on military and strategic questions." Now, this diary of Mr. Simic describes a meeting with the Presidency, which is dated on the 2nd of September, which is close to that date, but not the same date, in which at least Mr. Mladic speaks as well, just as General Gvero. Do you have any recollection whether around that date you had one meeting where Mr. Mladic and Mr. Gvero attended, whether there were two meetings in which Mr. Mladic and Mr. Gvero were present? And do you remember, if it was only one, whether Mr. Simic also attended that meeting; or, if there were two, if in one of them Mr. Simic attended?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are probably referring to this other document that I am supposed to be given now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked Mr. Registrar to print that out, and I first gave you the minutes of the 27th Session. I draw your attention to it that it's not the same date. There is --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I remember one conference that General Mladic held with his corps commanders in Bijeljina, to which he invited all of us, so that we could attend his briefing. I was there in Bijeljina, and I remember that meeting because of an incident involving Mr. Mauzer who held a rank of major, and Mladic ripped off his major's insignia and gave them to somebody else. But I couldn't otherwise remember what happened at that meeting, except that every commander gave a briefing about the situation in his area, what was going on, what they needed. I remember two such conferences that I attended. I believe that this is one of them. I don't think that it could be something else. They called it a briefing or a conference, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- so that would not be the same as a meeting of the Presidency, the 27th Session, although Mladic and Gvero were reported to be present there as well? This must be a different one?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
