utterances.text: No. This is the meeting to which they came. We were discussing these issues, and they came in the middle of the meeting. They probably joined the work. The issue here was a change of the constitution, and Mr. Trbojevic was raising some issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although it's reported that Mr. Mladic and Mr. Gvero also reported at the very end of that meeting on the 31st of August. But I now understand that this could not be the same -- could not have been the same meeting. Now, at the end of the 27th Session of the Presidency, it says that: "The generals briefed the Presidency in detail on military and strategic questions, the state, and the position of military units, equipment, and other questions." And then it continues, saying that: "All details were discussed, but they were not put on the record because of the level of their confidentiality." What exactly was so confidential at that time that it could not be put on the record?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was secret. When something is written this way, it gives free rein to imagination. This recording secretary wrote down all they said, but they always said things like they need money, they need equipment, they complained nobody was helping them, we are at these and those positions, we lack men. There is nothing else that he could have said. I remember those meetings. There were two or three of them at most. The meetings that we, from the leadership, had with representatives of the Main Staff. In Bijeljina, on the other hand, the whole -- the whole military establishment was there, and we came there as guests, to see what they're talking about. I don't know. I mean, I don't remember that there was anything in particular. It's just the way it's written. The woman who was taking these notes just wrote it that way. Because if they -- they had something special to say, they wouldn't have just come in the middle of the session. They would have come at the beginning, they would have provided background material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's move to the -- to the diary. Mr. Usher, could you please provide this to Mr. Krajisnik. If you would look at the third of the pages that is handed out to you, Mr. Krajisnik, last three digits 447 in your language. You see that Mr. Simic has written down something after "President of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik." I slowly read it. "Talking to the senior officers to," and then a word illegible, "movement for Yugoslavia. Senior officers are distancing themselves from the SDS. People think that whoever is against SDS is against Serbs. Senior officers are not inclined to the church. They are -- there are objections that the senior officers are meddling in authority. Equal partnership must be established between civil and military authorities. In case paramilitary forces should be formed, 80 per cent is the fault of the army and 20 per cent is the fault of the civilian authorities. Discipline must be established and anarchy, looting, and such things prevented." If this reflects what you said, Mr. Krajisnik, could you then explain exactly what that means: "In case paramilitary forces should be formed, 80 per cent is the fault of the army and 20 per cent is the fault of the civilian authorities"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unable to make any of this out. Just give me a second, please. No. It says: "If paramilitary forces -- if paramilitary units are being formed." If paramilitary units are being formed I said that it's 80 per cent the fault of the army -- I mean, I don't know exactly what I said but -- other corps commanders should have been present there. Yes, yes, you see there, Novakovic. All the corps commanders were present and we discussed our relationship. There was president of the municipality of Lopari. I remember it was a large gathering. This SK movement for Yugoslavia is a political party that tried to be a successor of the communist party, and it found some support among the military. And I probably mentioned that in terms of a certain mistrust existing. I don't know -- I don't believe that I could have said something like this, but probably I did say something when I was there. I remember they had a lot of critical remarks. Gvero, for instance, he was saying that civilian authorities did not function in certain places. They were blaming civilian authorities for certain things that were happening on the ground, and they required some measures to be taken to investigate, to identify, to establish all the negative things. Probably if we read this through, we could find it, because Gvero was in charge of morale and political affairs in the army and he had certain criticism to address to municipal authorities. This was a discussion about our mutual operation and coordination [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What kind of coordination you had in mind when you say: "Our mutual cooperation" -- at least I did hear "cooperation" and not operation, but I'm not quite sure what --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note Mr. Krajisnik said mutual functioning or mutual operation.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an army is a component in the war, it has to cooperate with civilian authorities. If there is a rift between them and the civilian authorities want soldiers to work in factories and the army wants them to man the trenches, if there is such a divide, it is impossible to work and to function if there is no coordination between civilian authorities and the army. But very often it boiled down to mutual accusations and assigning of blame on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what was your specific role as a Speaker of the Assembly of which, if I understood you well, you often emphasised that its role was limited and clearly to be separated from government and Presidency, what was exactly your role to be present during such a meeting which was very much discussing military matters?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was president of the Assembly. Very often representatives of the Main Staff attended Assembly sessions, so of course if they invited me there and if certain problems were being raised, it was quite natural for me to contribute to the discussion. I wasn't saying things like Howitzers should be used to fire at this or that or military actions should be taken here or there. I was discussing issues that I knew something about. It's always the role of a person who comes to attend a meeting as a guest. Naturally, I wasn't a guest in the true sense of the word. I was a representative of Republika Srpska, but I did take part in the discussion on issues that were familiar to me. I didn't discuss things like we need to take this territory or that territory. I don't think it was even mentioned. But it was important to identify who will play first violin, the army or the civilians. And it was a recurring problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In that diary, just below where you speak, the strategic goals come up.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As we find it also in the transcript of the 12th of July, 2005. What was the importance of addressing the issue of strategic goals at specifically that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very frequently many organs, many agencies, were saying: What do we want? Why is somebody fighting in different ways? And it's probably the case that the point here was to state what our goals were as a republic. I don't know whether these are my words; they probably are. But we were probably trying to say: These are the goals that the Assembly endorsed and the goals that we advocate at every peace conference. This is precisely from the beginning of September when the work on Vance-Owen Plan was just starting, and this gathering was probably anxious to know what the talks were about and what our objectives were. Objectives can be pursued in different ways, but I assure you -- and even the soldiers always emphasised that. Objectives always have to -- attained by political agreement. In the end they did not achieve any of these goals, apart from getting Republika Srpska. But the primary goal was for all goals to be attained by political means, and it was stated and restated at every conference. There must have been a proposal made here -- or rather, an attempt to foresee what the latest conference would propose, because what was topical at the time was one form of the Vance-Owen Plan that did not envisage Republika Srpska as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've talked a lot about -- and I'm moving to another subject. We talked a lot about Presidency meetings, guests being present. You also described informal contacts between members of the Presidency, and you said: "They found the time to talk to each other, so I do believe we would sit down for a cup of coffee and discuss certain matters, but I'm not quite sure, perhaps while we were on the way somewhere." Just to get an impression on how much of the time you spent together. I'm talking about five persons; that is, Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, Djeric, and you, how much of your discussions is finally put on record? I mean, the portion we see in the minutes, how much is that approximately of what you'd discussed among yourselves? I'm not qualifying -- not saying Presidency or expanded Presidency sessions, but those people -- or at least three, four, perhaps five of them. I mean, to what extent do we have a view on what was really discussed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll start with the easier question. For instance, the Prime Minister was based in a different location, and our meetings were rare. All these meetings that are recorded are probably the sum of all meetings, because he had to come from a distance of 15, 20 kilometres. As for Mrs. Plavsic, she had moved out to Belgrade and she would come occasionally and then go back. She would also travel across Republika Srpska, so that perhaps in later years the contacts were more frequent. But in 1992 I believe the meetings were rather few and far between. And if all of us attended these meetings, there were probably fewer of them because she left in May and already in July she was in Belgrade. As for Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic, all of us worked on our jobs during the day. We would either receive citizens or prepare papers. So all of us were doing our respective jobs, but we would also take walks together and discuss all sorts of things. And at those meetings we had, we discussed all the same subjects over and over again. There were no subjects that were left out. There were no official meetings where we would sit down, start a meeting, and say: Let's discuss this subject now. It was rather the case that if anybody had a problem they would consult with the others and finally a decision would be made. We spent a lot of time with representatives of foreigners, I used to call them, but representatives of the international community. We would sit down and discuss with them the current problems. That was the prevailing atmosphere. I see now that I didn't know about a lot of decisions that they had made, just as they didn't know about my decisions that I had made during the day because we were involved in different jobs. But if something was brought up at a meeting, then it was known to everyone. I gave you the example of Branko Simic on the 9th of November. I consulted them and then sent a letter. Then there was this problem of convoys not being able to pass, and that was brought to Radovan Karadzic and his assistant of sort. Mrs. Plavsic once came and said: We have a delegation from London, can Radovan attend a meeting with them if we receive them? That was our day-to-day work. And if I can now be allowed to say what I worked on, I did a lot of work. People just came to me with their needs. I would hear them out, talk to them, and then I would say: I'm now going to dial a number and direct you to see this or that person who could possibly help you. But I couldn't, myself, resolve any problems because I didn't have the right instruments; instead, I would call up the Prime Minister or somebody else and suggest a solution. And also we spent a lot of time working and preparing for conferences. If all our talks had been recorded -- I mean, it's all very similar to what is recorded. The discussions are the same, about politics. We didn't have any other topics, just politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give a few examples -- you said: "Now I know about a lot of decisions they had made," you are not aware of at that time. Could you give some major decisions which you were not aware of at the time, so not about appointments or -- major decisions that were decisive for the developments at the time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, I didn't know about a single decision taken by the government concerning appointments, launching of companies, maybe orders, because the government was far away from me and I didn't think I should know about it. I read about them here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you're referring to the government. I was mainly focussing on -- on -- let's say the five, without qualifying them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant Djeric. That's easiest to explain because he was far away. He issued an order, sent some ministers out into the field, sent out a report that I wasn't aware about because that was his job. As for Karadzic, there's a quite large number of laws that the government presented directly to Karadzic, he signed them, and they were published, and I didn't know about that process. Later, when the laws were promulgated they would be sent to the Assembly. For instance, the law about the expanded Presidency; I didn't know about that one. I didn't know about the clemency granted to three foreign citizens; French as it turns out. I didn't know about some appointment of some councillor or other. I didn't know about orders. I have now a book of orders. I didn't know a single one of them at the time, but they were issued by people in whose jurisdiction it was. Of course it was his job and it was his privilege. He had his advisor, he would issue orders, and I didn't have to know about that. As for Mr. Koljevic I didn't know about his meetings with Mr. MacKenzie about what they had agreed concerning the airport. Mrs. Plavsic also brought many issues to discuss with Mr. Karadzic without me. There are lots of examples. For instance, declarations and especially statements that people made to the press or the public. Of course everyone worked within their area of competence. It was not my area of competence and I didn't do those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, just a question which is related to your last answer; therefore, I've not prepared from any source. But I take it that this confirms again that you said: I was not involved in the negotiations on the airport agreement. Is that a correct understanding? Because there is evidence which goes in a different direction.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely wrong, absolutely wrong. I had nothing to do with the airport. That's not a problem; that's a positive thing. But I know exactly who it was. I mean, had I been involved, I would have said that I was. But no, I had nothing to do with the airport. I don't even know the man who testified here. I don't know -- well, perhaps I sat with him, but I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then a different subject, brief question. You explained to us that the Serb Assembly that was established would discuss various problems and adopt certain recommendations to the councilmen in terms of the areas where they were outvoted. That's what you said on the -- on the 28th of April. When reading the activities of the Serb Assembly -- also right in the beginning, let's say, for example, the 2nd Session, I read that there is a lot of attention to legislation, constitution, et cetera, and not just recommendations for Serb Assemblymen in areas they were outvoted. The activities, as described, very much reflect an active effort to establish instruments one would usually find in a functioning state. Could you clarify why you said it was mainly functioning as a -- well, just as a forum to discuss and to see how -- to adopt recommendations in the area, as -- where the Assemblymen were outvoted, whereas on paper it gives quite a different picture?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the Republic Assembly, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Serbian Assembly in the early stages --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic Assembly? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was then called the Serb Assembly of -- well, let's say not the BiH Republic Assembly, but there where the Assembly members would discuss, as you said, and adopt recommendations to the councilmen in terms of the areas where they were outvoted.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know how this was translated. Please, there was a recommendation to Municipal Assemblies. As for the Republican Serb Assembly, if I can call it that for short, it was established on the 19th, on the 19th of October, 1991. On the 14th of October, when this outvoting took place, in violation of the constitution, we called upon the other side asking them to withdraw that decision by 5.00 on the 19th and then we would not establish this Assembly. Once we established the Assembly, we stated publicly: MPs will work in the joint Assembly, while this Assembly will only decide on questions that are of vital interest to the Serb people. That was the month of October. Things were moving fast. First of all, the other side did not give a positive response. They went along with secession. The 15th of December happened, the European community asked their questions, and everything went in terms of us going in different directions rather than in the same direction. The Serb Assembly in Bosnia-Herzegovina started assuming the role of a real Assembly, rather than discussing only questions where the MPs had been outvoted. Things were moving in the direction of independent Bosnia; there was no agreement. There is a proper sequence of events. Now I just remembered something. On the 21st of November -- on the 21st of November, we had an Assembly meeting. The Presidency and the government, in spite of the fact that there was no agreement on the part of Serb representatives, they adopted a request for Bosnia-Herzegovina to ask for independence. Then everything went in a different direction. Then the Serb Assembly started working as any other Assembly rather than just confining itself to what was written down in the declaration on its establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps my question was not very clear. What you did, as a matter of fact, on the 28th of April, when you described what it meant to create Serb Assemblies, that you compared the functioning -- you said that would be called a Serb Assembly that could, and then you make a comparison, just like the Republican Assembly, which I understood to be just like the Republican Serb Assembly, discuss various problems and adopt certain recommendations to the councilmen in terms of the areas where they were outvoted. So you made a comparison of the functioning of the Republican Serb Assembly and the municipal Serbian Assemblies. Therefore, that's the reason why I noted that -- at least at the Republican level in very early stages it very much went in the direction of putting great emphasis on creating legislation, talking about constitution, et cetera. Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, later, yes. But the establishment was exactly the way it was, as I've said just now, what the point was of both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm almost finished. I've got two relatively short questions. The Deputies' Club was, at least at one occasion, used as a place where instructions would be given in the -- you have been -- it has been -- you were asked about -- well, as a matter of fact, it was on the 10th of May parts of the -- I think it was the 12th Assembly Session was read to you, part of it being a speech by Mr. Karadzic, who said: "The police must be under the control of the civilian authorities. It must obey it. There's no discussion about that. That's the way it must be. I think we shall hear it today in the form of instructions at the Deputies' Club." Which suggests that the Deputies' Club was a place where instructions were issued which then, I take it, were not issued at the Assembly meetings. Could you tell us, first of all, whether you were aware of this; and second, what you could tell us about the Deputies' Club as a place where important matters were dealt which finally were not in a similar way dealt with in -- or not at all perhaps, in a public Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is probably the 12th of May, right? It's not the 12th Assembly. It's the 16th Assembly in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could check it. If you continue -- let's just assume that you're right and I'm wrong, which is a likely possibility, then I'll check that right away. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. As far as the Deputies' Club is concerned, the Deputies' Club in the Serb Assembly was a talk shop. We'd have an agenda, and then people would talk about their problems. They would engage in discussions. They would take views. And perhaps they'd use up a lot of energy at the Deputies' Club. Every deputy on his own was an Assembly. There was no solidarity, there was no respect. Quite simply, people would often oppose many things. As for these instructions, that is the police being under civilian government, it probably has to be before the month of May. What is meant is that the police cannot be autonomous. It probably has to be under the minister, under the government, I don't know how I could explain this in a different way. It is unbelievable how, in a war, everybody wants to be a power in his own right and not to have anyone above him. The president of the club chaired the meetings and the deputy president sat next to him. They always honoured their guests, like Karadzic, Plavsic, Djeric, and I don't know who else - I was not a guest - if they were supposed to explain something. I would take the floor like everyone else. Of course I cannot say that they did not set store by what I had to say, but very often they would pass decisions that were different from my views. Quite simply, they thought that that is what democracy was. For instance, I so insisted on this declaration on the establishment of Republika Srpska on the 9th of January should be conditional, that is to say only if Bosnia is proclaimed as such, then it should enter into force; however, I had to relent because they insisted to such a great extent. There are these two examples and many other important examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the 12th Session on the 24th of March, which I referred to, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the MUP was established, yes -- or rather, when the law was established about the MUP probably and when the minister was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what happened all during that. I'm just referring to this specific portion where Mr. Karadzic said that further instructions, that one would hear about that in the form of instructions at the Deputies' Club. I have one or more -- one or two more questions for you, but we'll have to need a break. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention one point. It may be helpful to raise it before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the very end of yesterday's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's page -- sorry, it's 26.109 of the continuous transcript, but it's page 81. It's the very last page of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour put this question, it was the very last question of the day. "Yes, Mr. Mandic also testified that he specifically informed you about all matters in his knowledge, including irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities. Could you confirm this or ..." And then Mr. Krajisnik's answer included his disputing or disagreeing with what Your Honour had said, and then the clock intervened and the law of the clock applied to Your Honour, and that's where we were. My question is this, just it might be helpful over the break, I wonder if Your Honour was working from a specific transcript reference there because, if so, it would be most helpful to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had several in my mind, but if it would assist you, then it might be that I haven't got them with me at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's why I raised it before the break in case it was helpful to Your Honour to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly have them somewhere on my desk, which does not necessarily mean that it's easy to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I know that feeling, Your Honour, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a look at it, what I had exactly in mind, and where we find information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's much appreciated, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the parties should be prepared that I will be finished soon after the break. We'll adjourn until ten minutes past 6.00, and I apologise for being such a bad manager of time when you put the questions yourself to a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked for some information, pages on which I find relevant information in relation to this are 8.932 up till 33, then 9.072 to 74, and 9.376. These are the -- the -- I had the first one on my mind, but I find on the others information as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, let's -- let me put the last few questions to you. Yes, I've got only one question left. And let me just see where we were with the last one. Yes, I don't know whether I fully understood how the Deputies' Club could function as an instrument where matters were -- such as these instructions -- and today we earlier heard your testimony that in the Deputies' Club -- at least that's what I understood that you got the -- you gained the impression in the Deputies' Club also that the atmosphere was such that you couldn't move on when we were talking about the appointment of judges, that a lot of substantial matters were dealt with not in public but mainly in these secluded meetings, which makes it not that easy to follow exactly all the movements and to interpret what was done in public then. If you would like to assist me in further understanding, you're invited to do so. But if you say: Well, I said whatever I could say about it, then it's -- I would then move on.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Deputies' Club had the agenda of the Assembly. Very often this was sort of a night before the first night. However, it was a talk shop, too, as I said. People put different questions, there were discussions, and there was this energy that was used. You could feel what the views were with regard to certain issues, what the thinking of the deputies was regarding things that would be on the agenda of the Assembly the next day. The atmosphere was more relaxed, but it was an official meeting, that is to say it was chaired by the president of the club, people asked for the floor, there were discussions, and of course certain positions were taken at the Deputies' Club. It wasn't that positions were not taken and that conclusions were not drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and -- of course we heard a lot about it, but there are no minutes of those meetings; they were not in public.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. There are a few meetings, say, of the club that - well, how should I put this? - they were sort of similar. What was discussed at the Assembly was discussed at the club, too. I don't think it was too secret. People were sort of relaxed there. They could talk freely, as opposed to the Assembly where they weighed every word. Now, that may be the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Were at such meetings or at Assembly meetings, did it often happen that hard copies of documents were distributed, and it would not surprise you that I'm thinking about the distribution of the 19th of December instructions. Did it happen frequently that such documents were distributed and then, perhaps more specifically, distributed in numbered versions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Variants A and B were not distributed at the club as a club. Now, if this was a joint meeting with the SDS -- and perhaps it was distributed there, now that's possible. But if somebody distributed that at the club, no instructions were given at club meetings. I mean in writing. I do not remember a single case. I mean, apart from A and B. I don't remember any other such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I -- but I was not clear in that respect. I was referring to whatever kind of meetings in this atmosphere, so would it be -- you said already not in deputy club meetings but Main Board meetings -- well, whatever organ, either of the -- the state not yet established or the entity not yet established or organs of the party. I mean, please understand the question to cover all kind of meetings we have discussed over the last years. Would it happen at other meetings that such documents were handed out, and especially more specifically that they were numbered when distributed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember a single document of that nature having been distributed. When I spoke of Variants A and B -- well, if it was distributed. That was a meeting of the Deputies' Club and the Main Board, together. So if it was distributed, it could have been distributed at that meeting prior to the session itself. However, when club meetings were held as such, and that was most often the case, there were never any instructions given, apart from the agenda of the Assembly itself. I do not recall any such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Then finally a very short question. A question was put to you in relation to an answer you gave to Hasan Brkic, who was a journalist at Tesanj. He asked you: "What fund is being used to pay for arming the Bosnian Serbs with Kragujevac weapons? Do you know anything about that?" And then your answer was: "I don't know. I think they are being armed, but if such a fund exists, then really -- I think that the question is more of a provocative one." And then you later explained that your answer was provocative as well. I didn't understand that. In this answer, what's the provocation, apart from blaming the journalist for provoking you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if a journalist asks me, I don't even know when I said that or where, if he's asking me from what funds the Serb people are being armed rather than asking me whether the Serb people are being armed and do you have funds for that, well, then I would have taken it as a non-provocation. But if he's asking me from what funds, I took that as a provocation, because he's accusing you in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: I gave a provocative answer. What is provocative in that answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered in the same tone. I don't know, you can read the answer, the same tone. I pretended not to realise what this was all about, so I used the same tone but for me it was a provocative question because he's accusing you, what funds? Meaning to say that that was correct. I mean, why would I give that kind of answer to Hasan Brkic from those funds, if I knew? I don't even know who this Hasan is and when I stated that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. These were my questions. Is there any need to put further questions to Mr. Krajisnik? I have a few procedural matters as well, but -- which would take I don't think more than ten minutes. So we would have 20 minutes remaining. Have the questions of the Bench triggered any need to put further questions to Mr. Krajisnik? Mr. Josse? Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think normally the Prosecution get asked first, unless they say no, are they? I don't ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- well, you see, it's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Defence witness, so I think the questions should be asked first of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we usually --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we normally do it the other way round. We -- I thought this had been resolved, Your Honour, that in the same way that they get to cross-examine our witness and we get to re-examine. By the same token, we'd done it that way -- I thought we had a ruling at some point that that was the same procedure when it came to questions arising out of Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first make an inventory whether there's any need to put further questions to the -- to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There will be on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, in that case, Your Honour, may we respond to that when the Prosecution have put their questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I don't have a clear memory how we did it, which is very bad for a Presiding Judge, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean we don't need to go further. The Prosecution is prepared to go first. On the other hand, I will say the question before everyone is whether the questions of the Bench have prompted any need to ask additional questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the party who called the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Defence can certainly respond to that before it hears the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can respond to that by saying that at the moment we don't. But, Your Honour, that is, with respect -- whether the Bench's questions ultimately have given rise to the need for questions from the Defence in Mr. Krajisnik's interests is a question that can only finally be answered when we have heard the Prosecution's questions arising out of the Bench's questions. That is a correct and fair way of approaching it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will just have to check on the basis of the transcripts. I -- could I say spontaneously I addressed the Defence, and I'm old enough to be aware that sometimes you make mistakes. So therefore I'll review whether that's the practice --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment the Defence has not expressed any need for further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The reason I put it that way, Your Honour, is because that is our position at the moment. If the Prosecution have no questions, we have no questions, but I didn't want it to be understood that that would necessarily remain our position if the Prosecution do ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- well, let's get started, that's one; and the Chamber reserves a final determination to make on the basis of what we've done over the last few months and -- in relation to witnesses called by the Defence. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will ask a few questions of Mr. Krajisnik, and then my colleague, Mr. Tieger, will ask additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krajisnik. I wanted to turn to the topic of arming and specifically the to your evidence yesterday when you were asked by Judge Hanoteau whether or not you felt that information was being hidden from you on the subject of whether the Serbs were receiving arms. That testimony was -- the question was found at 14:49:10 of yesterday's transcript. Your answer, Mr. Krajisnik, was that you didn't have the impression that people with whom you cooperated, Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, and Mr. Karadzic, were keeping things from you. And you further answered that, and I quote: "I was not really informed whether somebody was shipping weapons by trailer from some other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina." That answer being found at 14:51:45. Then Judge Hanoteau directed your attention, Mr. Krajisnik, to the incident that occurred in Bileca on the 24th of May, 1991, where a member of parliament and a member of the SDS Main Board Dusan Kozic was detained by the police, eight crates of automatic weapons, 16.800 bullets, a pistol, 78 bullets for a pistol were found. And the MUP prepared a report, a copy of which is an exhibit in this case; it's P1213. You said that you had never heard of that report. In your evidence on the 7th of June, 2006, at page 25.296, line 17, you asserted, Mr. Krajisnik, that there had been some talk in the corridors of the Assembly, but that you "had heard nothing and I didn't even know it was Kozic." At page 25.297, lines 1 through 3 you testified: "There was no discussion about this, and this person was not identified as Kozic. Now I see it's Kozic. Well, probably it was. I don't know about this." Judge Hanoteau asked you yesterday at 14:57:20 if you believed that the minister of the interior wanted to hide the reality from you. And, Mr. Krajisnik, your answer at 14:58:46 was: "If it were an official piece of information, it would have had to be filed to Assembly. The Assembly would have forwarded it to the Prosecutor's office, and then things would have run their course." Contrary, Mr. Krajisnik, to your assertions that you were only vaguely aware about an incident in Bileca and that you were unaware that Dusan Kozic was involved in this incident, the contrary is true, Mr. Krajisnik. You were, in fact, informed officially by the MUP in your capacity as the Assembly president of this incident, weren't you, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I listen to you, I really could not link this up in the sense of me having said that because the Judge asked me whether they were hiding some information from me. I said that I had the impression that the people around me were not, and that was not linked to arming and to Kozic. Then I talked about Kozic, and I said that in the Assembly, in the corridors, there was this news. And I told you what the course the MUP should have taken in order to resolve this problem. I don't know whether the translation is different, but this is so confusing. Please tell me; I was telling you what the procedure was that the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina should have followed. They didn't have to send anything to me. They could have only sent it -- they should only have sent it to the prosecutor's office. I didn't know about -- well, of course I knew about Kozic, but Kozic wasn't at the Assembly at that time. I didn't know whether he did that or not because the other day Mr. Karadzic was at the press conference, and then that was stated. I have no idea how all of this is being interpreted, but in the Assembly this was not an official piece of information that was debated. That's what I said. Now, what you stated here and now, I'm sorry, but this is really a totally disparate. I can explain things -- I can explain everything. I didn't know that they were being armed. I knew that there was a case of -- in Bilic, the MUP did not inform me. The MUP was supposed to inform the Assembly, government, whatever. That's what I said yesterday and that is what I assert today. They could have sent information to the cabinet, but not to me. I mean, why would this go to Krajisnik? It should go to the prosecutor's office, and especially if they wanted to file criminal charges. I mean, I'm not hiding anything. I knew of the Bileca case. That's not a problem. I said that over here, too, and I know of another case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in addition to being informed by the MUP about this specific incident, you were informed about it by several people from Bileca as well, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, nothing, that's not correct. The MUP didn't inform me and nobody from Bileca informed me. Well, sort of by way of a story but that was much later, after Karadzic's press conference. But no, at that time, no, they did not inform me. Why would they inform me? I mean, they have the prosecutor's office, for heaven's sake, they informed the prosecutor's office and they initiated procedure. Who am I for that? No one informed me. Karadzic had his press conference on another day. You saw that press conference and it was no secret and it had to do with a completely different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, finally you personally had a discussion with Mr. Kozic about the arming allegations that had been made against him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember. Possibly. I do not remember. I do not remember having done that, but it's possible. Maybe much later, not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How much later, Mr. Krajisnik, would you have had a discussion with Mr. Kozic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: A week? Two weeks? A month?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He hadn't been to the Assembly for almost two months, if I remember correctly. He hadn't been at the Assembly for quite a while, and after that he grew a beard. I remember that. He didn't come to Sarajevo. I mean, if I talked to him. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So after May 24th, it would have been almost two months before you talked to Mr. Kozic about the event?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could distribute the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have it. Let's have it, this exhibit, and then I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This next exhibit, Your Honours, is an exhibit -- it is a newspaper article taken from Oslobodjenje on the 29th of May, 1991. The headline of which is "Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the SR BH Assembly on Bileca case." Subject: "Everybody should answer." And I refer Your Honours to the second paragraph on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, in the B/C/S it's found right in the middle of the page. It is in bold print, "Neka Svi Odgovaraju" is the title of it. And you can see your name above that in smaller upper case letters. I will read this. It says in the bottom of the first paragraph: "Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the SR BH Assembly, stated for Oslobodjenje and added: There is no justification for the creation of paramilitary formations despite the existing weaknesses in activities of the young coalition, which are frequently used to justify the actions of self-organisation, self-protection, and within these frames, also illegal arming. In this specific case of Bileca of which I was informed as president of the Republic Assembly both officially by the BH MUP and verbally on a couple of occasions by several people from Bileca, regardless of their opposing opinions, I can say that I am in favour of the law being implemented and everybody answering for their own actions without exceptions. This is also valid (if the court considers this case and finds him guilty) for Dusan Kozic, an SDS deputy in the SR BH Assembly, with whom I talked personally and who told me that on that occasion that he had found himself there by accident but once he was in that situation he tried to prevent the transport and distribution of weapons." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you were fully informed about this incident by the proper authorities. Isn't that correct? Does this article refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just tell you this: It says in Bileca they have opposing opinions, and he has a different opinion. My position is clear. I was informed only in corridors, not at the Assembly. It should have been presented to the Assembly officially, and that's what I said. And you can see what my position is from this, if this is really so. This is the Muslim Oslobodjenje. They must have told the truth. I don't know. This is the 29th of May. I don't know when the shipping of weapons took place. It's impossible that I had talked to him within five days, because he hadn't attended the Assembly for two months. There is a sequence, and you can see that he didn't come for two months. I don't know how this is possible because he didn't attend the Assembly sessions at that time, nor did he come to Sarajevo. But this is my position. It was my position then, and I later said it on TV that nobody can arm themselves without being held responsible. And there is again a little piece of news in a box here, a statement of MUP concerning the shipment of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just focus on the question that I asked you. The question I asked you, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first, Mr. Harmon, could we first -- is this what you told Oslobodjenje? So apart from how to interpret it, but is this approximately what you told them, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This corresponds to my position that there may not be any paramilitary units and it's impossible for people not to answer for their actions. I don't know what I said and what I answered and I don't remember giving that statement, that is to say I don't remember it now. But that is my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this incident took place on the 20 -- this interview or this newspaper article is dated the 29th of May, 1991. The incident took place on the 24th of May, 1991. Whether or not you had a -- strike that. Mr. Krajisnik, do you now -- does this article refresh your recollection in any way, Mr. Krajisnik, about this event in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I knew about the Bileca case, and I know that MUP submitted some sort of report. I didn't know the details. I did not discuss this with anybody in Bileca. I don't know how they could say that I did. That they -- they say here that they have opposing views, but I didn't hear about the details of how it happened, neither from them nor from the MUP. It's probably the truth, I don't know anymore now. MUP should have filed a criminal report, and that would be the end of it. The MUP doesn't explain why they did not file a criminal report to the prosecutor's office, that is. What do I have to do with it except that I gave a statement is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in your evidence and your answer to Judge Hanoteau at 14:58:46 you said: "If it were an official piece of information, it would have had to be filed to Assembly, the Assembly would have forwarded it to the prosecutor's office, and things would have run their course." That was your evidence according to the transcript, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's not what I said. I said if there had been a piece of information, it would have gone to the government, and from the government to the Assembly. But it's not the Assembly that can give it to the prosecutor's office. That sort of thing does not exist. I said the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what you said, Mr. Krajisnik, will be verified on the basis of the audio transcript so that we know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the necessary action to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I did say that, it was a slip of the tongue. The minister gives it to the government and the government to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the office of the prosecutor. What does the Assembly have to do with it? I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you said: I didn't say that. I said we would verify that. If there -- if it's different, then we'll look at whether it was the slip of the tongue or not, but let's first verify what it is and not speculate on anything else. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you. This needs an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg you, Mr. President, just one word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, I'm sorry to come back on this, but I'm reading the transcript and you have answered a question that was asked to you. [In English] "There was no discussion about this, and this person was not identified as Kozic. Now" -- now we are in the court now, "I see it is Kozic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will review my own video recording. At that time, it was not identified -- I didn't know it was Kozic at this moment, but you will see tomorrow that -- I mean, the next day Karadzic gave a press conference and mentioned Kozic as having found himself there by chance. I'll check it on the video recording and see exactly what I said about it. And it cannot be sent to the Assembly. Just tell me, please, what date so that I can check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The testimony was given on the 7th of June, 2006, and -- although it might not assist you, but perhaps if you have the page numbers it is -- it's page 25.297, and that is approximately at 10 per cent of the transcript of that day. And we'll pay specific attention to that. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is also another reference at 25.296, at line 17 as well, from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that's -- yes, there it says: "I heard of nothing and I didn't even know it was Kozic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, correct. At that time I didn't know anything, but later on you gave me the press conference given by Karadzic, you know, when we discussed those automatic weapons. I'll see the recording and see -- and see what I said and I'll inform you. I'll give you the exact description of what it was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check a -- one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you're checking, Your Honour, the press conference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- no, Mr. -- I'm just looking at -- because you made reference at that time to Assembly sessions. The question was: "So how did you become aware of this incident" -- oh, no, it's -- I haven't the full agenda of the 1991 Assembly sessions, I'm afraid. I do not know exactly when sessions were held in 1991, BiH Assembly, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave it to you, Mr. President, all the Assembly sessions, no problems. I provided all the Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was never on the agenda, not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not talking about whether it was on the agenda; I'm mainly trying to orient myself on the basis of your testimony where you said: We had a session of the Assembly, then deputies in the corridor started discussing this, et cetera, et cetera. And then -- so you're locating the rumours at the time of an Assembly session, which would then have to be anything between the 24th and the -- well, first coming Assembly sessions. And I just do not have a full --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll check that, too. I'll check that, too, and I'll inform you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a look at it. At the same time -- yes. No further questions, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. I do need an exhibit number for that last exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1260, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought Mr. Tieger was -- I'm not changing sides, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Tieger, when I ignored your importance, then I apologise for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I expect to be brief, but not that brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, not that brief. And I have a few procedural matters to discuss -- no, not to discuss, to -- yes, a few procedural matters. I'll try to be as briefly as I can. First of all, has the Prosecution considered what its position would be on the admission of the totality or parts of Mr. Karadzic's notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, we have, Your Honour. And the Prosecution is seeking the admission of that document in its totality. I know the Court has been referring to it as the -- maybe -- actually, maybe we're talking about two different documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about P1148.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me make sure I -- we're talking about precisely the same thing. That's the handwritten document, Your Honour? It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the -- I'd have to look quickly at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would need more time, perhaps you could already inform the Defence on what your position will be and see whether there is any disagreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can see the document now. That is a document to which we've been referring. I've had discussions --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I interrupt simply to say that Mr. Tieger did speak to me earlier. I think it would be helpful, bearing in mind we are going to be here tomorrow, if this was adjourned until tomorrow, and I will consider it further overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then yesterday you indicated that as far as the letter written by Mr. Karadzic to the Defence is concerned, where the Defence did not adopt it but neither did object against admission into evidence, you said that you would get back to the Court very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll get back to the Court right now, Your Honour. Yes, we do oppose its admission. There is no procedural rule that permits a statement such as that to come in. So we oppose it. It isn't a 92 bis statement, it's not attested to by a court officer. Under those circumstances, we oppose its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that if -- the Chamber would appreciate if the Defence would -- would say not only we do not object but we do not adopt the document either, whether they would take a position in view of what the objections by the OTP are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we -- for practical purposes I think we know our position, but, Your Honour, it seems sensible in the circumstances. Can we consider it and give our position in the morning? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Then we turn into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, before -- should I -- I have got a small point to raise in open session. Should I get that out of the way first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll return into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. They're separate entirely, appropriately open session points, Your Honour, I'm raising now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had two other ones as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm so sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one being that D254, that is the transcript of -- and translation of a -- of a video. Mr. Josse, I think you addressed the Chamber through an e-mail -- the Chamber staff to see whether the Chamber would really insist on having it all transcribed, being it's subtitled and whether not a more practical solution could be reached. The Chamber is always open for practical solutions. At the same time, if you could communicate a matter with the OTP, if the parties would come with a shared solution for the problem, we'll certainly -- it might be more easy for us to consider it and to follow that, compared to the situation where it's only one party who would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll speak to my learned friends about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So D254 is in the freezer at this point -- in the fridge for the time being until we have heard from the parties whether any agreement -- could we -- well, let's say a week should be sufficient to deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then finally I've got one very technical matter to pronounce. That is an issue about Nielsen source material. On the 27th of March, the Chamber directed the Prosecution to submit the source material cited in paragraph 347 of the report of expert witness Christian Nielsen. Specifically, the Chamber requested documents which, according to the report, were received by the Presidency. On the 25th of April, the Prosecution provided four such documents. On the 10th of May, the Defence filed a submission, to the effect that three of the documents had already been admitted into evidence. The Defence stated that it had no objection to the admission of the remaining document. The source material provided by the Prosecution consisted of the following documents, which have been assigned provisional exhibit numbers. P1177.A is a report on, I quote: "Some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead," which is dated the 11th July, 1992. This document has already been admitted into evidence numerous times under exhibit numbers P447; P529, tab 454; and P583, tab 77. P1177.B is correspondence from the deputy minister for police affairs, dated the 8th of August, 1992. This document has already been admitted into evidence as exhibit number P583, tab 84. P1177.C is a report from the Ministry of the Interior, dated the 22nd September 1992. This document is not yet in evidence. P1177.D is information about the involvement and activities of the Ministry of the Interior in the area covered by the Bijeljina security services centre, dated the 2nd of August, 1992. This document is similar to Exhibit P776; however, it includes a cover letter which is not in evidence. The Chamber hereby instructs the registrar to vacate exhibit numbers P1177.A through P1177.D, and to re-assign exhibit numbers P1177.A and P1177.B to the 22nd of September, 1992 report of the Ministry of the Interior, and the 2nd of August, 1992 report of the Ministry of the Interior, including a cover letter. And this concludes the Chamber's order. Next time when the Chamber invites one of the parties to provide additional material, the Chamber will at least make a serious effort to find out whether it's asking for something that is already in evidence, be assured of that. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the first point was only to clear up a possible misunderstanding that we thought might have arisen in relation to those inventories. I had said that the Defence had done some work of its own, which is true, but I wanted to make it clear, Your Honour, that we are not proposing to submit any of those items ourselves or to adopt them, and we haven't done full translations, except for one in any case. So, Your Honour, it's just that we're not -- we're not providing those translations. With respect, we're not doing that. So if anyone wishes to have that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I think if one of the purposes was that if Mr. Krajisnik wanted to further explain why some of these documents were really of importance that we at least would know what we are talking about, and therefore I asked the inventories to be translated first for the parties to see whether they would adopt any of these exhibits. We see that many of them are already in evidence, but also to give Mr. Krajisnik an opportunity to further explain why this Chamber, although the parties have not seen the importance of it, should really look at some or -- some of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I understand that's Your Honour's understanding. We're not at all being difficult. The Defence is not providing translations; it is not providing that service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then we have to look tomorrow at what we -- what we do have and what we do not have. I think I promised Mr. Krajisnik that at the end he could add whatever he thought of importance to add to his testimony, so an opportunity will be given tomorrow. If there are no other questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That last question of Your Honour's has dealt with my second point, Your Honour. I was seeking confirmation of exactly that. So I have nothing more to say this evening. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, yes, Mr. Krajisnik, we are late in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can say this in open session. May I receive the CDs that the Defence and the Prosecution have got?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say that we were going to make that request, that that should happen as soon as Mr. Krajisnik's evidence is finally completed, which would be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be most likely tomorrow. Mr. Krajisnik, you'll most likely receive the CDs tomorrow -- at least they are available to you tomorrow because then the -- the blockade of contact, although not real concrete blockade it was, but the functional blockade will be over and then there's no problem anymore. This then concludes the hearing for today. We'll start tomorrow, 9.30. We hope, Mr. Krajisnik, that you'll not have to suffer too much from the dentist. It's common human experience what it can be and sometimes it's not too bad. We'll start at 9.30. We'll have a longer break on from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a longer break of approximately one hour and a half, starting at a quarter to 11.00, so we have five quarters of an hour to start with. Then we'll resume after most likely approximately one hour and a half, and then see how much more time we would need. But I take it that we'll easily finish tomorrow with these matters. I apologise to the interpreters and the technicians for, again, bad time management. And we'll adjourn until tomorrow, 9.30, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of June, 2006, at 9.30 a.m.
